en: The Questions of Milinda:
The Book of Puzzles,
Chapter on the Refutation of Objections.
4. The Question on the Absence of Harsh Speech “Venerable Nāgasena, this was said by the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma:
‘Friends, the Tathāgata’s verbal conduct is completely pure; there is no verbal misconduct in the Tathāgata that he would need to guard against, thinking: “May people not...”’”
"May another person understand this of me.

Furthermore, when the Tathāgata was prescribing the *pārājika* offense for the elder Sudinna, son of Kalandaka, he addressed him with harsh words, calling him a "foolish man" (*moghapurisa*). And because of that address as a "foolish man," that elder—
Because he was constrained by a shrinking mind, he felt remorse and was unable to penetrate the Noble Path.
"Venerable Nāgasena, if the Tathāgata’s verbal conduct is pure and there is no misconduct in speech for the Tathāgata,
then why did the Tathāgata address the Elder Sudinna, son of Kalandaka, with the words 'foolish man' on account of his offense?"
The statement "it was customary" is false.
If it was customary for the Blessed One to address the elder Sudinna Kalandaputta with the term "foolish man" on account of his offense, then the claim that "the Tathāgata is pure in verbal conduct;
there is no verbal misconduct in the Tathāgata" is also false.
“This too is a double-pronged question that has come to you; it must be resolved by you.
“Great King, this was indeed said by the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma:

‘Friend, the Tathāgata’s verbal conduct is utterly pure. There is no verbal misconduct in the Tathāgata such that he would need to guard himself, thinking: "Lest another should find out this of mine."'”

When the Blessed One, in prescribing the *pārājika* offense for the Venerable Sudinna Kalandaputta due to his transgression, addressed him with the term "foolish person" (*moghapurisa*), he did so with a mind free from malice, without intent to provoke, and according to the actual characteristic of the case.

And what, Great King, is that actual characteristic? For whatever person, in this present existence, lacks the realization of the Four Noble Truths, his status as a man is "in vain" (*moghā*) because one thing being done turns out to be another; therefore, he is called a "foolish person."
“Thus, Great King, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Sudinna, the son of Kalandaka, with words that were true to his nature, not with false speech.

“But, venerable Nāgasena, even if one speaks truthfully while reviling another, we impose a fine of a kahāpaṇa upon him; for he who reviles, having committed an offense, is merely practicing a separate mode of conduct based on that matter.
“But have you ever heard before, Great King, of anyone bowing down to, rising up for, honoring, or presenting gifts to one who has stumbled?”

“Certainly not, venerable sir. One who has stumbled anywhere for any reason deserves reproach and deserves censure; they even cut off his head, kill him, bind him, have him executed, or have him burned.
“In that case, Great King, it appears that the Blessed One performed only an action, not a non-action.
“But even when performing an action, venerable Nāgasena, it must be done in a fitting and appropriate manner, even in the way he spoke.”
“Venerable Nāgasena, the world with its devas feels awe and shame before the Tathāgata; they desire even more to see him, to approach him, and to attend upon him.
“But, great king, does a physician give emollient medicines when the humors in the body have become stagnant and provoked?”
“Certainly not, Bhante; he does not give sharp writing instruments as medicine.

“In the same way, Great King, the Tathāgata gives instruction for the pacification of all the diseases of the defilements. Even though the Tathāgata’s speech may be harsh, Great King, it endears beings and makes them gentle.
Just as, Great King, even hot water softens whatever needs softening and makes it pliant;”
In the same way, Great King, even harsh speech from the Tathāgata is meaningful and accompanied by compassion.
Just as, Great King, a father’s words are meaningful for his children and accompanied by compassion,
even so, Great King, even harsh speech from the Tathāgata is meaningful and accompanied by compassion.
"Even harsh speech, O Great King, serves to abandon the defilements of sentient beings for the Tathāgata.
Just as, O Great King, even foul-smelling cow's urine when drunk, or even a bitter-tasting medicine when consumed, destroys the disease of sentient beings;
even so, O Great King, even the harsh speech of the Tathāgata is purposeful and accompanied by compassion."
"Just as, O Great King, even a large heap of cotton, having fallen upon another's body, causes no pain;
even so, O Great King, even harsh speech from the Tathāgata does not produce suffering in anyone.
"Well-analyzed, Bhante Nāgasena, is this question by many reasons."
“Excellent, venerable Nāgasena! It is so; thus do I accept it.
This is the fourth dilemma: on the absence of harsh speech.
